--- title: "AI agent workloads and service catalog on Google Cloud" description: "The workloads of a governed multi-agent platform: ADK and A2A agents, MCP tool servers and gateways, wired together by a declarative service catalog in env.yaml." --- # 1.0 Workloads, Catalog & Gateways — Overview (Layer 5) In the [Overview](../index.md), our loan officer asked a simple question: ***"Can you verify Julian Sterling's income?"*** Before we look at the security checkpoints (Section 2) or the cloud landing zone beneath the floor (Section 3), **Section 1 introduces the cast of workloads on stage (`layer-5-workloads`)**—the agents, tool microservices, and private front door that collaborate to answer that question—and shows how a single declarative **service catalog** (`catalog` in `env.yaml`) wires them together without coupling the teams that build them. --- ## 1. Four Teams, One Seamless Conversation Imagine how a traditional bank processes Julian Sterling's mortgage application. A customer relationship manager takes the borrower's request, hands the file to a specialized mortgage underwriter, and the underwriter checks three internal systems: the document vault (W-2s and tax returns), the payroll verification service, and corporate email. Esmeralda mirrors that exact organizational structure in software. Instead of cramming every prompt, database credential, and API integration into one giant "Mega-Agent," **Layer 5 splits the work across four independent tracks**, each living in its own isolated GCP project: | Track / Team | Role in Julian Sterling's Request | GCP Project | Layer 5 Units | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **CX Product Team** | Owns the customer conversation. Builds the **orchestrator** agent (`cx-mortgage-orchestrator`, Google ADK) that greets the loan officer and delegates specialized work. | `esm--cx-agents-` | `agents/cx-mortgage-orchestrator` | | **AI CoE Team** | Owns reusable domain intelligence. Builds the **mortgage specialist** (`ai-coe-mortgage-specialist`), published over the **Agent-to-Agent (A2A)** protocol so any business unit can invoke it. | `esm--ai-coe-agents-` | `agents/ai-coe-mortgage-specialist` | | **Backend / MCP Tools Team** | Wraps core enterprise systems as standardized **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** microservices on private Cloud Run. | `esm--mcps-` | `services/legacy-dms`, `services/income-verification`, `services/corporate-email` | | **Gateway / PlatformOps Team** | Operates the private front door (**entry point** at `*.esmeralda.internal`), routing traffic via the built-in `direct` backend or optional adapters (`envoy`, `apigee`). | `esm--gateway-` | `entrypoint`, `gateways/direct`, `gateways/envoy` | Neither agent team needs network peering or IAM admin rights in the other's project. Every call from an agent leaves through the **Central Agent Gateway** (Layer 4) and arrives at the target through the **private entry point** (`*.esmeralda.internal`): ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph CX["CX Team Project (modules/5-workloads/agents/adk-agent)"] Orch["cx-mortgage-orchestrator
(Reasoning Engine, BYOC)"] end AGW["Central Agent Gateway
(Governance Project, Layer 4)"] subgraph Gateway["Gateway Project (modules/5-workloads/entrypoint + gateways/direct)"] EP["Entry Point
internal HTTPS LB
*.esmeralda.internal"] PSC["PSC NEG
(region-aiplatform.googleapis.com)"] Adapter["Optional Adapter
(e.g. Envoy, off by default)"] EP ==> PSC EP -.-> Adapter end subgraph CoE["AI CoE Team Project (modules/5-workloads/agents/a2a-agent)"] Spec["ai-coe-mortgage-specialist
(Reasoning Engine, BYOC)"] DB[(Cloud SQL Postgres)] Spec -.-> DB end subgraph MCPServers["MCPs Project (modules/5-workloads/services/* + serverless NEGs)"] M1["corporate-email"] M2["income-verification"] M3["legacy-dms"] end Orch ==>|"1. A2A: ai-coe-mortgage-specialist.esmeralda.internal"| AGW Spec ==>|"2. MCP: #60;svc#62;.esmeralda.internal/mcp"| AGW AGW ==> EP PSC ==>|"Host + path rewrite, caller's access token"| Spec EP ==>|"Serverless NEG, caller's ID token"| MCPServers ``` --- ## 2. Why We Designed It This Way: Key Decisions & Trade-offs Why separate orchestrators, specialists, MCP tools, and gateways into distinct Layer 5 units? Here is the summary of the architectural decisions behind Section 1: | Decision | Why We Made It | What We Avoided | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **ADR-04: Standalone MCP Microservices Instead of In-Process Python Functions** | Exposes every enterprise connector (`legacy-dms`, `income-verification`, `corporate-email`) as an independent FastMCP service on Cloud Run that scales to zero and has its own IAM invoker list and `Agent Registry` entry. | Redeploying and re-evaluating the entire AI agent every time a backend SQL query or API schema changes; granting the agent raw database credentials. | | **ADR-05: Multi-Agent Delegation (A2A) Over a Single Mega-Prompt** | Splits customer conversation (`cx-mortgage-orchestrator`) from domain underwriting (`ai-coe-mortgage-specialist`) using the open A2A protocol and published Agent Cards. | Context-window pollution, inflated token costs, degraded tool-selection accuracy, and duplicate underwriting logic across multiple customer channels. | | **ADR-06: Automated VPC-Internal Database Bootstrapping** | Provisions the specialist's private Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance alongside an ephemeral VPC-bound Cloud Run Job (`-db-bootstrap-`) that grants IAM database privileges automatically during deployment. | Public database IPs, manual `psql` steps from developer laptops, or long-lived bastion VMs. | | **Declarative Service Catalog (`catalog` in `env.yaml`)** | Defines every private host, its workload kind (`mcp`, `a2a`, `adk`), its credential type (`id` vs `access`), its health probe, and its authorized `callers` in one file. | Scattering hostname mappings, IAM invoker bindings, and smoke-test scripts across dozens of unrelated Terraform files. | --- ## 3. How It Works & CLI in Practice ### The Layer 5 Deployment Order When you deploy Layer 5 (`uv run esmeralda deploy --layer 5 --env dev`, shortcut `make deploy-workloads ENV=dev`), the CLI applies every enabled unit one by one in the order derived from their Terragrunt dependency blocks, each through the destroy guard, and stops at the first failure. The order has six stages: 1. **AI Reasoning Engines** (`agents/ai-coe-mortgage-specialist`, `agents/cx-mortgage-orchestrator`) — Deploys the BYOC containers on Vertex AI Agent Runtime, binds them to the Layer 4 Central Agent Gateway, and registers the specialist's `A2A_AGENT_CARD`. 2. **MCP Tool Services** (`services/{legacy-dms,income-verification,corporate-email}`) — Deploys the private Cloud Run containers and registers their `TOOL_SPEC` schemas (`tools.json`) in the central **Agent Registry**. They come after the agents because they read each agent's identity for `run.invoker` and their caller guard. 3. **Gateway Backends** (`gateways/direct` always, plus any enabled adapter in `gateways.enabled` such as `gateways/envoy`) — Creates the serverless NEGs and Private Service Connect NEGs pointing at the deployed services and agent engine IDs. 4. **Private Entry Point** (`entrypoint`) — Configures the internal HTTPS load balancer (`*.esmeralda.internal`) using the reserved IP and DNS zone from Layer 2 and the internal Root CA leaf certificate from Layer 3. 5. **Verification Test VM** (`test-vm`) — Provisions the private IAP-tunneled runner VM used by `uv run esmeralda verify` (`make test-gateway`) to probe every catalog route from inside the Shared VPC. 6. **IAP Egress Grants** (`iap-egress`, always last) — Registers the catalog's external (`managed: false`) targets in the Agent Registry and grants `roles/iap.egressor` on each Agent Registry entry to the callers the catalog lists, so the agents' SPIFFE identities are authorized to egress through the Central Agent Gateway to exactly those destinations. After the last unit, the deploy runs the running-image check (`uv run esmeralda build --verify --env dev`, skip it with `--skip-verify-images`). ### Operating Layer 5 with the `esmeralda` CLI You can inspect, test, build, deploy, and verify every Layer 5 workload directly from the CLI: ```bash # List all Layer 5 units and live catalog routing uv run esmeralda units --env dev uv run esmeralda status --env dev # Run Julian Sterling's underwriting query locally (--local-mcp starts and stops the local MCP servers) uv run esmeralda query --agent-dir apps/agents/cx-mortgage-orchestrator --local-mcp \ "Can you verify Julian Sterling's income?" # Plan or apply a specific Layer 5 workload unit (with destroy-guard protection) uv run esmeralda plan layer-5-workloads/services/income-verification --env dev uv run esmeralda apply layer-5-workloads/services/income-verification --env dev # Build and push one image, then deploy its unit uv run esmeralda build income-verification-api uv run esmeralda deploy services/income-verification --env dev # Plan all of Layer 5 read-only, then deploy it uv run esmeralda deploy --layer 5 --env dev --dry-run uv run esmeralda deploy --layer 5 --env dev # Verify all *.esmeralda.internal routes and run a live end-to-end orchestrator query uv run esmeralda verify --env dev ``` --- ## Subsections in Section 1 Follow Julian Sterling's request through the five subsections of Section 1: 1. **[1.1 Two Teams, Two Agents — Orchestration vs. Specialization (ADK & A2A)](./03-ai-agents-and-database.md)** * Meet `cx-mortgage-orchestrator` (Google ADK) and `ai-coe-mortgage-specialist` (A2A). * Why they live in separate GCP projects, how BYOC on Vertex AI Agent Runtime works, and how the zero-bastion Cloud SQL task store is bootstrapped. 2. **[1.2 Wrapping Enterprise Systems as MCP Tool Servers](./02-mcp-tool-servers.md)** * Meet `legacy-dms`, `income-verification`, and `corporate-email` on private Cloud Run. * How `tools.json` contracts register in the Agent Registry, how caller ID tokens flow end-to-end, and how developers test tools locally. 3. **[1.3 The Private Front Door & Pluggable Gateways](./01-ingress-gateways.md)** * How the `*.esmeralda.internal` entry point routes traffic with the built-in `direct` backend (zero extra proxy VMs). * How teams can plug in **Envoy** or **Apigee X** via `gateways` in `env.yaml` and migrate hosts one at a time without touching agent code. 4. **[1.4 Partner API Management & Token Monetization with Apigee X](./04-apigee-partner-gateway.md)** * Step-by-step walkthrough of how Apigee X (`partner.esmeralda.internal`, served on the entry point) exposes curated agents (`partner-agents`) and MCP tools (`partner-mcp`) to external B2B partners. * How `VerifyAPIKey`, KVM allowlists, two-phase `` (`EnforceOnly` + SSE `EventFlow` `CountOnly`), and `PostClientFlow` analytics work end-to-end with GEAP Agent Identity and the Central Agent Gateway. 5. **[1.5 One Gateway per Hop](./05-gateway-per-hop.md)** * Which gateway handles each hop by default (entry point, Central Agent Gateway, Apigee X, Envoy, API Gateway model routing), and when to choose an alternative. > [!TIP] > Curious how the outbound **Central Agent Gateway** verifies SPIFFE identities and private TLS certificates on every hop? After finishing Section 1, head to **[2.1 Central Agent Gateway & Private PKI](../3-agentops-and-lifecycle/01-central-agent-gateway.md)**.

--- title: "esmeralda Python library and CLI for agent platform operations" description: "The esmeralda runtime library (ADK plugin, telemetry, gateway trust) and CLI and MCP server for plans, guarded applies and end-to-end verification." --- # 4.0 The `esmeralda` Runtime & Operations Library ## 1. Keeping Every Agent at ~30 Lines of Pure Domain Logic Suppose an AI engineer on the CX team wants to add a new skill to `cx-mortgage-orchestrator` to help **Julian Sterling** compare mortgage rates, or the AI CoE team wants to launch a second specialist agent. What should that engineer's workday look like? Ideally, the engineer writes **~30 lines of pure domain logic**: an `agent/agent.py` file declaring the ADK `Agent`, its system instructions, and its tools or sub-agents, alongside a concise `agent.yaml` manifest. In reality, running an enterprise agent inside a zero-trust bank environment requires solving half a dozen thorny operational problems on every single container startup and request: * Installing the Layer 3 internal Root CA (`AGENT_GATEWAY_ROOT_CERTIFICATES`) into the Linux system trust store and Python's `certifi` bundle before any TLS connection opens. * Patching `google-genai` onto `httpx` and configuring `aiohttp` so every outbound call honors the Central Agent Gateway's HTTPS egress proxy. * Minting and caching Google ID tokens or OAuth2 access tokens, forwarding end-user OAuth tokens (`User-Auth-Token`), attaching the engine's SPIFFE identity (`X-Agent-Spiffe-Id`), and brokering 3-legged OAuth (3LO) credentials through Agent Identity Auth Manager (`esmeralda.auth_manager`). * Emitting structured FinOps token events (`genai_token_consumption`) and tool latency events (`mcp_tool_execution`), while propagating `caller.project_id` and `caller.agent_name` across OpenTelemetry spans. * Serving both `google-adk` (`adk api_server`) and `a2a` (A2A REST server with `AgentCard` URL pinning) identically on a workstation and in production. Before the `esmeralda` library existed, each agent carried its own copy-pasted `entrypoint.sh`, telemetry callbacks, and monkey-patches. Those copies inevitably drifted apart—and worse, code wired onto `AdkApp` subclasses never even executed when the container launched `adk api_server` or an A2A server in production. **We extracted [`packages/esmeralda`](../../../packages/esmeralda/README.md) (a uv workspace package in this repository, imported as `esmeralda`; see [Installing the package](#installing-the-package)) so agent authors never write plumbing code again—and platform operators get a single, unified CLI (`uv run esmeralda ...`) and MCP server (`esmeralda mcp`) to operate the entire repository.** ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph AgentCode["What the Agent Team Writes (~30 lines)"] A1["agent/agent.py
Pure ADK Agent, prompts & tool list"] A2["agent/__init__.py
esmeralda.prepare() + create_app(root_agent)"] A3["agent.yaml
framework (google-adk | a2a), env & local_env"] end subgraph RuntimeLib["What esmeralda Handles Automatically"] R1["Container & Process Lifecycle
• esmeralda run (installs Gateway Root CA)
• esmeralda.prepare() (httpx/aiohttp proxy patches)
• esmeralda serve (ADK API server or A2A server)"] R2["Zero-Trust Auth & Delegation
• esmeralda.mcp & esmeralda.a2a headers
• esmeralda.auth_manager (3LO Auth Manager + SPIFFE)
• esmeralda.mcp_authz (zero-latency JWT verification)"] R3["FinOps & Trace Telemetry
• EsmeraldaTelemetryPlugin (token & tool JSON events)
• BaggageSpanProcessor (caller.project_id / agent_name)"] R4["Platform Operations CLI & MCP
• esmeralda query (in-process, localhost, or remote engine)
• esmeralda status / doctor / units / plan / apply / verify / logs
• esmeralda contracts / guard / mcp (read-only agent server)"] end AgentCode ==> RuntimeLib ``` * **[Usage guide](guide.md):** step-by-step patterns for adding `esmeralda` to an agent, serving ADK/A2A workloads, calling MCP servers and remote agents, brokering 3LO tokens, querying agents, and operating a checkout with `esmeralda mcp`. * **[Package reference](reference.md):** complete API reference for every module, function, class, CLI subcommand, environment variable, and telemetry event schema. ### Installing the package The `esmeralda` package is not published on PyPI. Install it from this repository: * **From a checkout (recommended).** `uv sync` at the repository root installs it in the workspace; run the CLI with `uv run esmeralda --help`. The operations commands (`status`, `plan`, `apply`, `verify`, `mcp`, ...) act on that checkout. * **CLI on your `PATH`.** From the repository root, `uv tool install --editable packages/esmeralda` puts `esmeralda` on your `PATH` and follows your checkout as it changes. Add `--with fastmcp` if you want `esmeralda mcp` from that install (in the workspace, `fastmcp` comes from the lock). * **Runtime library in another project.** Install from Git: `uv pip install "git+https://github.com/google/esmeralda#subdirectory=packages/esmeralda"`. The package has no workspace-only dependencies, so it builds on its own. > [!NOTE] > A different, unrelated project already uses the name `esmeralda` on PyPI. `pip install esmeralda` does not install this package. --- ## 2. Why We Built It This Way (Key Decisions & Rationale) | Decision | Alternative Considered | Why We Chose This | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Shared Workspace Package (`packages/esmeralda` / `import esmeralda`)** | Copy-pasting `entrypoint.sh`, auth helpers, and OTel callbacks into each agent directory | Eliminates code drift across teams; keeps every agent's `agent/__init__.py` to 4 lines and `agent/agent.py` focused 100% on business prompts and tools. | | **Hook Only Universal Extension Points (`ENTRYPOINT`, import-time `prepare()`, ADK `App` plugin)** | Subclassing `AdkApp` or attaching per-agent `after_model_callback` | `adk api_server` and A2A servers bypass `AdkApp` subclasses in production. Using `esmeralda run` (`ENTRYPOINT`), `esmeralda.prepare()`, and `EsmeraldaTelemetryPlugin` guarantees identical behavior in Agent Runtime, Gemini Enterprise, A2A, and `adk web`. | | **Runtime CA Injection (`esmeralda run`) Instead of Baking Certs into Dockerfiles** | `COPY root-ca.crt` inside `Dockerfile` during `docker build` | Baking an environment's CA into the image breaks immutable promotion from `dev` to `prd`. Injecting `AGENT_GATEWAY_ROOT_CERTIFICATES` at deploy time lets the exact same image digest run in every environment. | | **Unified Runtime + Operations CLI (`uv run esmeralda ...` & `esmeralda mcp`)** | Separate bash scripts and raw `terragrunt`/`gcloud` one-liners | Gives human engineers (`esmeralda status/plan/apply/verify/query/logs`) and AI coding agents (`esmeralda mcp`) one structured, destroy-guarded interface backed by `esmeralda.ops`. | --- ## 3. Technical Architecture & In Practice ### Why Universal Extension Points Matter The library hooks only into extension points that execute in **every** serving mode (local in-process runs, `adk web`, `adk api_server`, A2A servers, and Vertex AI Agent Runtime): | Extension point | Runs in production because | |---|---| | Container `ENTRYPOINT` (`esmeralda run --`) | Docker always runs it before `CMD` (`esmeralda serve --otel-to-cloud`) | | Code executed when the agent package is imported (`esmeralda.prepare()`) | Every server imports the agent package to load the agent | | An ADK `App` with a plugin (`esmeralda.create_app(root_agent)`) | The ADK loader looks for `app` before `root_agent`; plugins run inside the ADK runner, whatever the API in front of it | ### The Four Stages of a Request's Life ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Container start: esmeralda run"] --> B["Agent package import: esmeralda.prepare()"] B --> C["First request: EsmeraldaTelemetryPlugin runs esmeralda.finalize()"] C --> D["Every request: EsmeraldaTelemetryPlugin callbacks"] ``` | Stage | When | What the library does | |---|---|---| | **Entrypoint** | Once, before the server process starts | Installs the Agent Gateway root CA into the system trust store and certifi, then `exec`s the server | | **prepare** | Once, when the agent package is imported, before the agent and its clients exist | Environment defaults; forces google-genai onto httpx and makes aiohttp honor the proxy env; points the genai client at the model location | | **finalize** | Once, when ADK and its telemetry providers exist | Registers the span processor that copies the caller context onto spans | | **Per request** | Every run of the ADK runner | Puts the caller context in OpenTelemetry baggage for the run; emits tool and token telemetry events | ### What You Get Out of the Box - **One image for every environment.** No certificate is baked in. The entrypoint installs the bundle that Terraform injects at deploy time, so the image digest tested in dev is the one promoted to prd. - **Egress through the gateway works out of the box.** google-genai, aiohttp and the genai client defaults are adjusted before any client is created. - **Telemetry in every serving mode.** The Agent Runtime query API, Gemini Enterprise, A2A and `adk web` all emit the same `mcp_tool_execution` and `genai_token_consumption` events. The Layer 4 log metrics and dashboards read them. - **Caller attribution.** Every span of a request carries `caller.project_id` and `caller.agent_name` when the caller identifies itself. Agent-to-agent calls do it automatically. - **One CLI for runtime and platform operations.** From `uv run esmeralda query` to `uv run esmeralda verify --env dev`, every developer and operator workflow runs through a single tested CLI. > [!IMPORTANT] > The caller context is whatever the caller sends. Use it for telemetry and cost attribution only, never for authorization.

--- title: "Cross-cloud identity for AI agents: workload identity federation" description: "Verify agents from other clouds without shared secrets: workload identity federation, OIDC claims checked at the gateway, SPIFFE federation, mTLS, and fail-closed rules." --- # 5.1 Identity Across Clouds Inside one Google Cloud organization, identity is easy to take for granted. When `cx-mortgage-orchestrator` calls `ai-coe-mortgage-specialist`, the Central Agent Gateway sees an attested SPIFFE `principal://` identity, and IAM sees a Google-issued token. Both were minted by the same platform that checks them. Now picture a new caller: an underwriting agent that a risk team runs on another cloud. It has an identity there (an IAM role, a managed identity, a Kubernetes service account), but Google Cloud did not issue it. Before that agent may touch Julian Sterling's file, Esmeralda needs to answer three questions: 1. **Can the identity be verified cryptographically**, without a shared secret or a long-lived key? 2. **Which team does it belong to**, so the call can be authorized and billed? 3. **What happens when either answer is missing?** The short answers: federated, signed tokens verified at the gateway; the catalog; and the call is denied. --- ## 1. The Rule: Attribution Comes from Authentication Every request can carry two kinds of information about its caller: | Kind | Example | Trusted For | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Verified identity** | A JWT signed by the caller's cloud and validated against that issuer's published keys; a federated principal minted by Google's Security Token Service; a client certificate chained to a trusted CA. | Authorization **and** chargeback. | | **Declared context** | A header or A2A metadata field saying `cost_center: cc-underwriting-example` or `agent_name: underwriter`. | Telemetry and reporting only, and only when the catalog allows that value for the verified caller. | Esmeralda never bills or authorizes on declared context alone. Self-asserted headers (such as an agent name in `X-API-Key`, or a SPIFFE ID copied into a custom header) stay telemetry-only. This is what makes cross-team, and now cross-cloud, chargeback impossible to fake. --- ## 2. Four Ways a Workload on Another Cloud Proves Who It Is ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Caller["Workload on another cloud"] W["Underwriting agent"] end W -->|"A. cloud OIDC token"| WIF["Workload Identity Federation
(Google STS token exchange)"] W -->|"B. cloud OIDC token"| GWJWT["Gateway verifies JWT
(issuer JWKS, audience)"] W -->|"C. SPIFFE SVID"| SPF["SPIFFE federation
(exchanged trust bundles)"] W -->|"D. client certificate"| MTLS["mTLS at a gateway
(trusted CA)"] WIF --> P1["principal://iam.googleapis.com/.../subject/SUB"] GWJWT --> P2["ISSUER#SUBJECT"] SPF --> P3["spiffe://TRUST_DOMAIN/PATH"] MTLS --> P4["certificate subject / SAN"] P1 & P2 & P3 & P4 --> CAT["Catalog caller
(identity → team)"] ``` | Pattern | How It Works | Verified Principal | Best Fit | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **A. Workload Identity Federation** | The workload exchanges a token from its own cloud (for example an AWS or Azure workload credential) with Google's Security Token Service through a [workload identity pool](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-other-clouds) and provider. It then calls Google Cloud APIs with a short-lived federated token, either directly or by impersonating a dedicated service account. | `principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects//locations/global/workloadIdentityPools//subject/` | Callers that need Google Cloud IAM directly (Cloud Run invoker, Vertex AI, BigQuery, the Telemetry API). | | **B. OIDC verified at the gateway** | The workload sends a JWT from its cloud's OIDC issuer. The gateway looks the issuer up in an allowlist, fetches its JWKS, and verifies signature, issuer, audience and expiry. | `#` | Inbound agent calls through Apigee (the cross-cloud best path), or Envoy with JWT verification. | | **C. SPIFFE federation** | Both sides run SPIFFE-compatible identity and exchange trust bundles, so each side can verify the other's SVIDs. | `spiffe:///` | Organizations that already standardized on SPIFFE across clouds and clusters. | | **D. mTLS** | The caller presents a client certificate at a gateway that terminates TLS and validates the chain against a trusted CA. | Certificate subject or SAN | Legacy or partner systems that cannot mint OIDC tokens. | > [!TIP] > Prefer keyless patterns (A, B, C). They rely on short-lived tokens signed by an identity provider you already operate, so there is no long-lived secret to rotate or leak. Use mTLS (D) when a system can only present certificates, and terminate it at a gateway rather than inside agent code. ### Why `issuer#subject` and Not Just `subject` A JWT `sub` claim is only unique **within its issuer**. Two clouds, or two tenants of the same cloud, can both issue a token with `sub: underwriter`. If the gateway keyed callers on `sub` alone, a workload from the wrong issuer could inherit another team's grants and bill another team's cost centre. Esmeralda therefore keys OIDC callers on the pair: the gateway composes `caller.identity = #` from the **verified** claims, and the catalog registers the same `(issuer, subject)` pair. Workload Identity Federation principals already encode both the pool (the trust relationship) and the subject in one string, so they need no extra composition. --- ## 3. Verifying an OIDC Caller at Apigee: The Cross-Cloud Shared Flow When `governance.capabilities.cross_cloud = "apigee"`, the Layer 5 Apigee `cross-cloud` unit manages an allowlist of trusted external issuers in an Apigee KeyValueMap (`kvm-cross-cloud-issuers`). Each entry maps a short issuer **slug** to three values: the issuer URI, the JWKS URI, and the expected audience: ```hcl # Illustrative: trusted issuers for the Apigee cross-cloud unit (synthetic values) trusted_issuers = { example-cloud = { issuer_uri = "https://oidc.example.com" jwks_uri = "https://oidc.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json" audience = "https://partner.esmeralda.internal" } } ``` The cross-cloud **shared flow** turns that allowlist into a fail-closed verification step that the partner proxies call before anything else is trusted: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Workload on another cloud participant P as Apigee partner proxy
(partner-agents / partner-mcp) participant SF as cross-cloud shared flow participant KVM as kvm-cross-cloud-issuers participant T as Target agent or MCP server C->>P: Request + x-api-key + x-cross-cloud-issuer: example-cloud + x-cross-cloud-token: JWT Note over P: AM-Strip-Verified-Headers removes any client-supplied x-verified-* headers P->>P: VerifyAPIKey (app, developer, product) P->>SF: FlowCallout (header present, or product/app requires cross-cloud) SF->>SF: Missing issuer or token? → 401 SF->>KVM: Look up issuer_uri, jwks_uri, audience for the slug SF->>SF: Unknown issuer? → 403 SF->>SF: VerifyJWT (signature via JWKS, issuer, audience, expiry) SF->>SF: Invalid token, or empty iss / sub? → 401 SF->>P: caller.identity = iss#sub, raw token removed P->>P: App owner_identity ≠ caller.identity? → 403 P->>T: Forward (Apigee's own Google credential), x-verified-identity set by the gateway P-->>P: ML-interaction record with caller_identity + caller_issuer ``` Three details make this path trustworthy: 1. **Spoof-proof headers.** The proxy strips every client-supplied `x-verified-*` header first, so the only `x-verified-identity` that can reach a target is the one the gateway set after verification. 2. **Key-to-identity binding.** A partner API key alone is not enough. When the developer app carries an `owner_identity` attribute, the proxy rejects the call (`403`) unless it matches the verified `iss#sub`. A leaked key is useless without a valid token from the right workload. 3. **The raw token stops at the gateway.** The shared flow removes the cross-cloud JWT before forwarding. Downstream services receive the verified identity, never the credential. > [!IMPORTANT] > The target behind Apigee (for example, an agent on Agent Runtime) authenticates **Apigee's** service identity, not the original caller's. That is by design: the gateway is the verification point, and the gateway's `ML-interaction` record is the **source of truth for attribution** on this path. Targets should not try to re-derive the caller from forwarded headers. --- ## 4. Registering a Federated Caller in the Catalog Verification answers *"is this token genuine?"* The catalog answers *"who is this, and what may they do?"* Every non-workload identity (a VM, a human group, a partner Apigee app, a SPIFFE ID, or a workload on another cloud) is declared under `callers`, mapped to the **team** that pays for its calls. A workload on another cloud is declared with identity type `federated` and its `(issuer, subject)` pair. In the team-owned `catalog/` layout, such entries live under `catalog/external/clouds/`, which platform and security own: ```yaml # catalog/external/clouds/example-cloud-underwriter.yaml (synthetic) schema: esmeralda.catalog schema_version: 1 teams: example-cloud-underwriting: description: Synthetic underwriting team running on another cloud. cost_centers: [cc-underwriting-example] country: BR external: true callers: aws-underwriter: team: example-cloud-underwriting description: Underwriting workload on another cloud (federated identity). identity: type: federated issuer: https://oidc.example.com subject: example-underwriter-role ``` The **target** owner then decides what that caller may do. The AI CoE grants it access to its specialist, through Apigee, under a specific API product and quota: ```yaml # catalog/teams/ai-coe/agents/ai-coe-mortgage-specialist.yaml (excerpt) callers: cx-mortgage-orchestrator: { cost_centers: [cc-cx-br, cc-cx-mx] } aws-underwriter: { gateway: apigee, product: gold, quota: { tokens_per_minute: 50000 } } ``` The other identity types follow the same shape: | Identity `type` | Required Fields | Example | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `federated` | `issuer`, `subject` | An OIDC workload on another cloud | | `spiffe` | `ref` (unit output) or `id` | `spiffe://example.org/ns/risk/sa/underwriter` | | `apigee_app` | `id` (and optional `product`) | A partner developer app | | `service_account` | `ref` (unit output) or `id` | A test VM or a platform workload | | `group` | `id` | An operator group | Identities the platform creates are referenced from Terraform unit outputs (`ref: layer-3-security:`), never pasted by hand. Identities owned elsewhere, such as an external issuer, are written as literals and reviewed by platform and security through CODEOWNERS. > [!NOTE] > The team-owned `catalog/` folder, the `federated` identity type and `esmeralda catalog resolve` / `show` are on `main` ([2.6 Service Catalog](../3-agentops-and-lifecycle/06-service-catalog.md)). Today only agents and `service_account` callers are compiled into enforcement (IAM grants); `federated` callers are resolved and shown, and compiling them into Apigee products and apps is planned. See [5.5 Status & Roadmap](./05-status-and-roadmap.md). --- ## 5. Fail Closed, at Every Step Every way a cross-cloud call can go wrong ends in a denial, never in an "allowed but unattributed" request: | Situation | Result | Where It Is Enforced | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | No credentials at all | `401` | Every hop: IAM, IAP, Apigee keys | | Issuer header or token missing where cross-cloud is required (by header, product or app attribute) | `401` | Apigee cross-cloud shared flow | | Issuer not in the trusted allowlist | `403` | Apigee cross-cloud shared flow | | Bad signature, wrong audience, expired token, or empty `iss` / `sub` | `401` | Apigee cross-cloud shared flow | | Valid key but `owner_identity` does not match the verified `iss#sub` | `403` | Apigee partner proxy | | Client tries to inject `x-verified-identity` | Header stripped; the binding check then fails | Apigee partner proxy | | Authenticated caller not in the catalog | Denied (`policy.attribution.unmapped_caller: deny`) | Gateway grants compiled from the catalog | | Declared cost centre not allowed for the caller | Rejected or billed to the caller's own team (`policy.attribution.declared_mismatch`) | Attribution views | The last two rows describe the catalog **policy**: ```yaml # catalog/policy.yaml (excerpt) policy: attribution: unmapped_caller: deny # deny | flag (allow + alert, e.g. a dev sandbox) declared_mismatch: reject # reject | bill_own_team ``` Because enforcement is **compiled** from the catalog, `unmapped_caller: deny` is a property of the build: a caller absent from the catalog never receives a gateway grant, an API product, or an IAM binding in the first place. And because being listed is what makes a caller billable, the "unattributed" count in the usage views has an expected value of zero, with an alert when it is ever greater ([5.3](./03-unified-observability-and-chargeback.md)). --- ## 6. The Outbound Direction: Esmeralda Agents Calling Other Clouds Identity also matters when `ai-coe-mortgage-specialist` calls *out* to a service on another cloud. The remote side wants proof of who is calling, and it should not have to trust a static API key. The keyless pattern mirrors pattern A in reverse: 1. The agent obtains a **Google-signed OIDC ID token** for its own service identity, with the remote service as the audience. 2. The remote cloud trusts Google as an OIDC identity provider and exchanges that token for its own short-lived credential (for example, assuming a role with a web identity, or a federated credential on an application registration). The trust policy pins the expected audience and the agent's subject. 3. The agent calls the remote service with the remote credential. The Central Agent Gateway governs every one of those calls: the remote service **and** the remote cloud's token-exchange endpoint must both be registered in the Agent Registry, or the gateway blocks them. Tokens travel as ordinary HTTP headers, so they pass through the gateway's inspection unchanged. > [!TIP] > Give each agent its own outbound identity. When several agents share one service account for outbound calls, no callee, on any cloud, can tell them apart, and per-agent attribution is lost. Per-agent identities are a prerequisite for verified attribution and are on the roadmap ([5.5](./05-status-and-roadmap.md)). --- **Next Subsection:** The caller is verified. Now, which path does its request take between clouds, and which gateway sits on each hop? Continue to **[5.2 Cross-Cloud Connectivity & Protocols](./02-cross-cloud-connectivity.md)**.

--- title: "Multi-cloud AI agent observability and token chargeback" description: "Normalize usage from agents on any cloud into the esmeralda.usage record with an OpenTelemetry adapter or Collector, land it in BigQuery, and charge back by team." --- # 5.3 Unified Observability & Chargeback In **[2.3 FinOps, Telemetry & Cross-Team Chargeback](../3-agentops-and-lifecycle/03-centralized-monitoring-and-dashboards.md)**, the CFO could see what Julian Sterling's mortgage inquiry cost, because every agent wrote structured telemetry into Cloud Logging and Layer 4 sank it into BigQuery. That worked because every producer was an Esmeralda agent on Google Cloud, using the same library. Multi-cloud breaks that assumption three ways at once: * The underwriting agent on another cloud is written in a **different framework**, maybe a different language. * Its telemetry lands in a **different cloud's** logging and tracing stack. * Its token usage is billed by a **different model provider**. If each producer describes usage its own way, FinOps ends up writing one parser per cloud, per framework, per gateway, and the numbers never quite add up. Esmeralda's answer is a **contract**: one normalized record that every producer emits, wherever it runs. --- ## 1. The Normalized Schema: `esmeralda.usage` Every unit of usage, from any producer, is one `esmeralda.usage` record. There are four event types: | Event | One Record Per | Typical Producer | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `llm.call` | Model call | The workload (agent library, span adapter) | | `tool.call` | Tool call | The workload | | `agent.invocation` | Agent run (with a token roll-up for budgets and alerts) | The workload | | `gateway.request` | Request crossing a gateway | Apigee, Envoy, or a mapped gateway log | Field names follow the [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) wherever they exist, so any OTel-instrumented framework already produces most of the data. Two fields make the record work across clouds: * **`workload.cloud`** (`gcp`, `aws`, `azure`, `on_prem`, `other`) and **`workload.runtime`** (`agent_engine`, `cloud_run`, `gke`, `external`) say *where* the work ran. * **`caller`** says *who* asked for it. `caller.principal` and `caller.team` count for chargeback **only** when `caller.verified` is `true`, meaning they came from authentication. Anything the caller merely claimed goes in `caller.declared`. Each record carries `schema: "esmeralda.usage"` and an integer `schema_version`. Additive changes keep the version; only a breaking change bumps it. Consumers select records by `schema`, never by log name, which is what lets records from any cloud and any transport land in the same tables. Records never contain credentials, tokens or the delegated user credential, in any field. > [!NOTE] > The `esmeralda.usage` contract (`contracts/usage-event.schema.json`), its Python producers and the Layer 4 usage views are in open pull requests. On `main`, agents emit the earlier `genai_token_consumption` and `mcp_tool_execution` events with OpenTelemetry baggage, read by `vw_monthly_agent_chargeback` (see [2.3](../3-agentops-and-lifecycle/03-centralized-monitoring-and-dashboards.md)). See [5.5 Status & Roadmap](./05-status-and-roadmap.md). --- ## 2. Producers on Every Cloud The contract is the same everywhere; only the producer changes. | Producer | Where It Runs | How It Emits `esmeralda.usage` | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **`esmeralda` library, ADK plugin** | Any Python ADK agent, on any cloud | `esmeralda.create_app(root_agent)` installs a telemetry plugin that emits `llm.call`, `tool.call` and `agent.invocation` records. | | **`esmeralda` library, OTel GenAI span adapter** | Any OTel-instrumented Python framework (LangGraph, LangChain, CrewAI, custom code) | `UsageSpanProcessor` on the `TracerProvider` maps finished GenAI spans to records. | | **`esmeralda` library, manual API** | Python code without ADK or OTel instrumentation | Typed builders such as `record_llm_call()` and `record_tool_call()`. | | **OpenTelemetry Collector** | Any language, any cloud | Receives OTLP from the workload and forwards records (or maps GenAI spans to records) to Google Cloud. | | **Apigee** | Inbound gateway | The `ML-interaction` message-logging policy writes gateway records with the verified caller. | | **Envoy** | Gateway adapter | A JSON access-log format that matches the schema. | | **Fixed-format gateways** (such as Agent Gateway logs) | Google Cloud | Mapped to the schema by a BigQuery view. | For a Python agent on another cloud, the span adapter is usually all it takes. The workload declares where it runs through environment variables (`ESMERALDA_CLOUD=aws`, `ESMERALDA_RUNTIME=external`, `ESMERALDA_TEAM=example-cloud-underwriting`) and switches the transport to OpenTelemetry logs so a collector can ship the records: ```python from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider from esmeralda.usage import UsageSpanProcessor # Environment: ESMERALDA_USAGE_TRANSPORT=otel, ESMERALDA_CLOUD=aws, ESMERALDA_RUNTIME=external provider = TracerProvider() provider.add_span_processor(UsageSpanProcessor(framework="langgraph")) ``` For workloads in other languages, an **OpenTelemetry Collector** is the bridge. The workload exports standard OTLP traces and logs to a collector on its own cloud; the collector exports to Google Cloud's OTLP endpoint (the Telemetry API, `telemetry.googleapis.com`), authenticating keylessly with a [Workload Identity Federation credential configuration](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-other-clouds) instead of a downloaded key. The federated principal needs only permission to write telemetry. ```yaml # Illustrative OpenTelemetry Collector config on the other cloud. # GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS points at a Workload Identity Federation # credential configuration file (no service account key). extensions: googleclientauth: {} receivers: otlp: protocols: http: {} exporters: otlphttp: endpoint: https://telemetry.googleapis.com encoding: proto auth: authenticator: googleclientauth service: extensions: [googleclientauth] pipelines: traces: { receivers: [otlp], exporters: [otlphttp] } logs: { receivers: [otlp], exporters: [otlphttp] } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph OC["Another cloud"] PY["Python agent
(esmeralda span adapter)"] ANY["Agent in any language

OTLP through a collector is the multi-cloud transport: the record is the same, only the envelope changes. A tested reference collector configuration (including a processor that maps GenAI spans to records for non-Python workloads) is on the roadmap; until then, treat the snippet above as a starting point and validate that the records arrive with `schema = "esmeralda.usage"` in the governance project. --- ## 3. Landing in BigQuery Layer 4's hub-and-spoke telemetry model extends naturally: records from Google Cloud spokes and from other clouds all reach the governance project, and one sink keyed on `jsonPayload.schema = "esmeralda.usage"` streams them into a BigQuery usage table. Views on top of it do the rest: 1. **Normalize.** Gateway and workload records, from any producer, are flattened into one shape. 2. **Join on `trace_id`.** A single request usually leaves several records: an Apigee `gateway.request` on the way in, `llm.call` and `tool.call` records from the specialist, and maybe an `llm.call` from the caller on its own cloud. W3C trace context propagation ([5.2 §3](./02-cross-cloud-connectivity.md#3-a2a-and-mcp-the-interoperable-protocols)) gives them all the same `trace_id`. 3. **Pick the billing source per hop.** When a gateway is on the hop, its record is the primary source for tokens and caller identity. Workload records add per-tool and sub-agent detail, and are the floor on `direct` hops. 4. **Accept only registered dimensions.** Business keys such as `loan_product` are accepted only if the catalog's `policy.dimensions` registers them. --- ## 4. Chargeback by Verified Team The goal of all this plumbing is a simple, defensible statement: **the team whose verified identity triggered the work pays for it**, wherever the work ran. | Question | Answered From | | :--- | :--- | | Who called? | `caller.principal` with `caller.verified = true` (an `iss#sub`, a federated principal, a SPIFFE ID, an Apigee app or a service account) | | Which team pays? | The catalog's `callers` / targets mapping of that principal to a team, compiled into an attribution table | | Which cost centre? | The caller's declared cost centre, only if the catalog allows it for that caller (`policy.attribution.declared_mismatch` decides otherwise) | | What did it cost? | Token counts from `llm.call` or `gateway.request` records (`usage.input_tokens` includes cached tokens; `usage.output_tokens` includes reasoning tokens) | | Where did it run? | `workload.cloud`, `workload.runtime`, `workload.team` | A month-end chargeback row for the worked example in [5.4](./04-bringing-an-agent-from-another-cloud.md) might read: | Calling Team (verified) | Serving Team | Serving Cloud | Requests | Input Tokens | Output Tokens | | :--- | :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | `example-cloud-underwriting` | `ai-coe` | `gcp` | 1,240 | 4,860,800 | 812,200 | | `cx` | `ai-coe` | `gcp` | 9,310 | 36,494,000 | 6,098,050 | *(Synthetic numbers.)* Two alarms keep the view honest: * **Unattributed usage.** Any record whose principal is not in the attribution table counts as unattributed. The expected value is zero; an alert fires when it is ever greater. * **Declared vs. verified mismatch.** A caller declaring a cost centre its team does not own is rejected or billed to its own team, per policy, and surfaced for review. > [!IMPORTANT] > Verified attribution needs every caller to present a **distinct** verified identity. On paths where the callee only sees a gateway's identity (such as a target behind Apigee), the gateway's record is the attribution source. Self-declared context (OpenTelemetry baggage such as `caller.project_id`, A2A caller metadata) stays useful for dashboards but never decides who pays. --- ## 5. Verified Attribution on Internal Hops, End to End This section follows one internal call from catalog entry to chargeback row: an agent or a platform identity calling an agent or an MCP server inside Google Cloud. The partner front door (Apigee apps and cross-cloud callers) uses the same table and policy and is documented separately as a follow-up. ### 5.1 Who the callee can verify, per hop | Hop | Verified identity | Read by | Deny enforced by | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Agent → agent or MCP server through the Agent Gateway | The calling agent's Agent Identity (`principal://…/reasoningEngines/`), proven by mTLS | The Agent Gateway's authorization decision (IAP egress audit record: principal, target, granted or denied) | Per-target `roles/iap.egressor` lists compiled from the catalog: a principal with no binding gets `403` at the gateway | | Any caller → MCP server on Cloud Run | The caller's Google ID token (`email`, or the service account's numeric id in `sub` when the token has no email claim). Cloud Run IAM validates it before the request reaches the container | The in-process **caller guard** (`esmeralda.attribution`) | Cloud Run `run.invoker` (catalog callers only), then the guard's allowlist | | Any caller → agent on Agent Runtime | The caller's access token, checked by Agent Runtime IAM. The container never receives the caller's credential | The Agent Gateway record only (when the caller is an agent) | `aiplatform.user` and the gateway lists; no in-process check is possible | | Humans and operators | Group membership | IAM | Group grants (the catalog maps the group to a team) | Self-asserted values (`X-Agent-Spiffe-Id`, `X-API-Key`, the A2A caller context) never count as verified. > [!NOTE] > **Why Agent Runtime records are attributed at the gateway, not in the process.** Agent Runtime authenticates the caller at its front end, then calls the agent's container with the platform's own credential. The caller's token never reaches the container, so no code in the agent can verify who called. The usage records an agent on Agent Runtime writes therefore always carry `caller.verified = false`, and the Agent Gateway's authorization record (verified principal and target) is what attributes the hop. For the same reason, the "unattributed" checks are split in two, each with an expected count of 0: > > * workload records from guarded workloads (`workload.runtime` other than `agent_engine`) without `caller.verified = true`; > * Agent Gateway decisions that let a principal through (`granted = true`) when that principal has no `principal_teams` row. ### 5.2 Catalog policy ```yaml # catalog/policy.yaml policy: attribution: unmapped_caller: deny # deny (403) | flag (allow, record unattributed, alert) declared_mismatch: reject # reject (403) | bill_own_team flag_environments: [dev] # flag is a resolve error anywhere else ``` `flag` only relaxes the in-process guard. Gateway and IAM grants always come from the catalog, so a caller that is not in the catalog has no grant in either mode. ### 5.3 What the catalog compiles `esmeralda catalog resolve --env --write` adds an `attribution` block to `catalog/.resolved/.json`: * **`principal_teams`**: one row per verified principal (`principal`, `principal_type`, `caller`, `team`, `cost_centers`). Each agent contributes its Agent Identity principal (`agent_runtime`), which is also the identity it calls out as. Callers contribute their identity (`group:` for groups); a caller identified by a unit output is included only when a target of the environment lists it. The Layer 5 `iap-egress` unit resolves the references and replaces the `source = catalog` rows of the Layer 4 `principal_teams` table in one transaction, only when the rows change. The usage views read that table through `vw_principal_teams`. * **`allowlists`**: for each guarded target (MCP servers and A2A agents), the principals the caller guard accepts, with the team and the cost centres each one may declare on that target. * **`shared_principals`**: identities several agents present (only from an optional `shared_workload_identity` policy block). Empty in this repository: since [#134](https://github.com/google/esmeralda/issues/134) each agent calls out with its own Agent Identity and is attributed by its own principal. A shared principal would not be in `principal_teams`; on a target it would resolve to a team only when every agent caller of that target belongs to the same team, otherwise the call is accepted but carries no team, and the gateway record decides who pays. The compiler also checks that **anything allowed is attributable**. A principal that would get a gateway or IAM grant without a `principal_teams` row, or one principal mapped to two teams, fails the build. ### 5.4 The caller guard The MCP servers wrap their app with the guard: `app = CallerGuard(app)`. Each one ships a byte-identical copy of the package module as `caller_guard.py`, because the module uses only the standard library. The guard reads its allowlist from `ESMERALDA_CALLER_ALLOWLIST`, which the service's Terraform unit writes from the compiled block (`env.yaml` `attribution.caller_guard`). The unit also writes: * `"token_validated_by": "cloud_run_iam"`. The service requires IAM invoker auth and internal ingress, so Cloud Run has already validated the identity header (`X-Serverless-Authorization`, else `Authorization`) when the request arrives. Behind the internal load balancer the token arrives with its signature. Without this setting the guard trusts only a token whose signature the platform removed. * **Trust assumption:** the unit sets it only for services with internal ingress and IAM invoker auth required (no `allUsers`). * The first identity header present decides. When `X-Serverless-Authorization` is present, `Authorization` is never read, even if the former is empty or unparseable: Cloud Run validates only `X-Serverless-Authorization` and passes `Authorization` through untouched. * An alias for every service-account entry under the account's numeric unique id. A Google ID token minted without the email claim (the VM metadata server's default format, an Apigee `GoogleIDToken` without `IncludeEmail`) names the account only in `sub`. Each decision is one JSON log line (`jsonPayload.event = "esmeralda.caller_decision"`, with `reason`, `principal`, `team`). Unverified decisions also log the shape of each identity header (`absent`, `opaque`, `jwt_signed`, `jwt_stripped`, `malformed`), never its value. For each request: | Situation | `deny` / `reject` | `flag` / `bill_own_team` | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | No validated identity (missing or malformed header; or a still-signed token where the platform's validation isn't declared) | `401` | Allowed, `caller.verified = false` | | Verified principal not in the allowlist | `403` | Allowed, principal recorded, no team | | Mapped principal declaring a cost centre (`X-Esmeralda-Cost-Center`) it may not use | `403` | Allowed, billed to its own team, `declared` keeps the claim | | Mapped principal | Allowed. `caller.verified = true`, `caller.principal`, `caller.team`; the response carries `X-Esmeralda-Billed-Team` | Same | `esmeralda serve` installs the same guard on A2A servers when an allowlist is configured, except on Agent Runtime, where the container can't see the caller. The ADK plugin then fills `caller.verified`, `caller.principal` and `caller.team` only from the guard's decision. ### 5.5 Proving it: `esmeralda verify` On top of the route probes, `esmeralda verify` runs two attribution probes from the test VM ([`scripts/vm/gateway_probes.sh`](../../../scripts/vm/gateway_probes.sh)): * **Unregistered caller:** the probe identity `sa-probe-unregistered-` is in no catalog entry and holds no role. The test VM can only mint its tokens. It calls every MCP and A2A host and must get `403`, in both `deny` and `flag`, because IAM and the Agent Gateway reject it before any caller guard. The probe reads the effective policy from the resolved catalog. If a host ever let the identity through to its guard, `deny` still requires `403`. Under `flag`, the call may succeed but must stay unattributed, and the probe warns that the IAM grant shouldn't exist. * **Declared mismatch:** the test VM declares another team's cost centre on every guarded MCP host. It must get `403` under `reject`, or `2xx` billed to its own team under `bill_own_team`. Both are controlled by `env.yaml` `attribution` (`unregistered_probe`, `caller_guard`): on in `dev`, off in `prd` until the rollout below is done there. ### 5.6 Rolling it out without locking out traffic 1. In `dev`, set `catalog/environments/dev.yaml` `policy.attribution.unmapped_caller: flag`. Redeploy the MCP services, run `esmeralda verify --env dev`, and check that the guard logged no `"reason": "unmapped"` or `"unverified"` decision (`esmeralda logs --env dev`). 2. Remove the override (deny), redeploy, and run `esmeralda verify --env dev` again, including the `403` probes. 3. Apply the `iap-egress` unit (`env.yaml` `attribution.principal_teams`). It loads the `principal_teams` rows and creates the gateway attribution count and alert. Both unattributed alerts are on by default (Layer 4 `alert_on_unattributed_usage`), each expecting 0. 4. Repeat in `prd` by enabling `attribution.caller_guard`, `attribution.unregistered_probe` and `attribution.principal_teams` in its `env.yaml` (`flag` is refused there). > [!NOTE] > The partner hop (Apigee apps and cross-cloud `iss#sub` callers) attributes from the gateway's `ML-interaction` record: the callee only sees the proxy's identity. Mapping those principals through the same `principal_teams` table, with the same `unmapped_caller` policy, is the next step. --- **Next Subsection:** Identity, connectivity and telemetry are in place. Let's put them together and onboard a real (synthetic) agent from another cloud, step by step. # Apigee Platform Module (`modules/5-workloads/apigee/platform`)

<!-- Adapted from github.com/ricardosmh/apigeex-terraform-deployment (Apache-2.0) -->

Agent Gateway is Esmeralda's governance plane for agent traffic. Apigee can optionally add API-management capabilities, such as partner access, API products and token quotas, through independent modules selected per capability in `env.yaml`.

## Overview

This module provisions the foundational Apigee X control plane and Private Service Connect (PSC) networking bridge required when one or more Apigee capabilities are enabled in `env.yaml`:

1. **Non-Peering PSC Organization (`byo_apigee_org = false` default)**:
   - Provisions `google_apigee_organization` with `disable_vpc_peering = true` (no `/22` VPC peering reservation required), `runtime_type = "CLOUD"`, configurable `billing_type` (`PAYG`, `EVALUATION`, or `SUBSCRIPTION`), and `retention = "MINIMUM"` on paid organizations.
   - Supports optional Cloud KMS customer-managed encryption keys (`enable_cmek = true`) and Analytics add-on configuration (`enable_analytics`: the environment's PAYG Analytics add-on that feeds the console dashboards and the stats API; `enable_advanced_api_ops`: the separate org-level Advanced API Ops add-on, off by default).
   - Supports Bring-Your-Own Apigee organization mode (`byo_apigee_org = true`) via `existing_org_id` and `existing_instance_service_attachment`.
2. **Instance, Environment & Environment Group**:
   - Provisions `google_apigee_instance` with PSC `consumer_accept_list`, `google_apigee_environment` (`BASE`, `INTERMEDIATE`, or `COMPREHENSIVE`), `google_apigee_envgroup`, and their attachments.
3. **Northbound Entrypoint Contract (Internal ALB -> Apigee)**:
   - Provisions a regional `PRIVATE_SERVICE_CONNECT` Network Endpoint Group targeting the Apigee instance service attachment and a regional `INTERNAL_MANAGED` HTTPS backend service (`timeout_sec = 300`).
   - Exposes `backend_service_id` and `routes` matching the `modules/5-workloads/entrypoint` gateway contract.
4. **Southbound Entrypoint Target Server (Apigee -> Entrypoint ILB)**:
   - When `entrypoint_service_attachment` is provided, provisions `google_apigee_endpoint_attachment` and `google_apigee_target_server` (`ts-esmeralda-entrypoint`) over HTTPS (port `443`) with strict TLS validation (`s_sl_info.enabled = true`, `ignore_validation_errors = false`).
5. **Proxy Runtime Identity**:
   - Provisions `sa-esmeralda-apigee-proxy-<env>` and grants `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` to the Apigee Service Agent (`service-<project_number>@gcp-sa-apigee.iam.gserviceaccount.com`) so deployed proxies can mint upstream `GoogleAccessToken` and `GoogleIDToken` credentials.
